title: Immortality in Folio
teaser: Shakespeare's colleagues rescue eighteen plays from oblivion. Galileo declares nature's language is mathematics. A new pope befriends science while Protestant armies die at Stadtlohn. Two roads to immortality — through art or through knowledge — converge in a single year.

art.label: Art
art.content: Gerard van Honthorst paints The Concert in Utrecht — a burst of candlelit color brought back from Rome. Honthorst had studied Caravaggio's chiaroscuro in Italy, earning the nickname Gherardo delle Notti (Gerard of the Nights) for his mastery of artificial light. Now the Utrecht Caravaggisti transplant that dramatic technique to Protestant Holland, where it will influence Rembrandt and the Dutch Golden Age. In Rome, Gian Lorenzo Bernini sculpts his intense Self-Portrait, all fierce eyes and flowing hair — the Baroque genius at twenty-four, already reshaping papal patronage. The Droeshout portrait engraved for Shakespeare's First Folio is awkward as art but priceless as document: the only contemporary image we have to verify against the poet's death mask.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: Seven years after Shakespeare's death, his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell publish Mr. William Shakespeare's Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies — the First Folio. Of the thirty-six plays collected, eighteen exist in no other source: Macbeth, The Tempest, Twelfth Night, Julius Caesar, and more would have vanished without this act of devotion. About 750 copies were printed; 235 survive today. Ben Jonson contributes a prefatory poem declaring Shakespeare 'not of an age, but for all time' — a prophecy fulfilled by the book that made it possible. In Spain, Pedro Calderón de la Barca debuts as a playwright with Amor, honor y poder, beginning a career that will rival Lope de Vega's.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: In October, Galileo publishes Il Saggiatore (The Assayer), dedicated to the newly elected Pope Urban VIII. The book's explicit argument concerns comets — and on that question Galileo is wrong. But its implicit argument reshapes knowledge itself: 'Philosophy is written in this grand book, the universe... It is written in the language of mathematics.' Where scholastics debated Aristotle's texts, Galileo insists we read nature directly through observation and geometry. This is the scientific revolution as epistemological rupture — not new facts alone, but a new way of knowing. Urban VIII, still an ally of science, receives the work with delight. Their friendship will not survive the decade.

hist.label: History
hist.content: On August 6th, two pivotal events coincide. In Rome, Cardinal Maffeo Barberini is elected Pope Urban VIII — a humanist, poet, and patron of Galileo who will transform Baroque Rome. At Stadtlohn in Westphalia, Tilly's Catholic League army destroys Christian of Brunswick's Protestant force: 6,000 dead, 4,000 captured, all artillery lost. The Battle of Stadtlohn ends the Palatinate phase of the Thirty Years' War, crushing Protestant hopes in the Empire. Frederick V, the 'Winter King' of Bohemia, abandons his campaigns. Maximilian of Bavaria gains the Palatinate's electoral vote. On June 19th, Blaise Pascal is born in Clermont — the future author of probability theory and the Pensées.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The year poses a question: how does meaning survive? Heminges and Condell answer through preservation — gathering scattered quartos and playhouse manuscripts into a single book, betting that print will outlast memory. Galileo answers through method — arguing that nature's truths, unlike texts, cannot be corrupted by copyists because mathematics transcends language. Urban VIII's election momentarily aligns Church and inquiry; the Barberini bees on Il Saggiatore's title page signal that Rome and science might be friends. Stadtlohn shows what happens when ideas fail to preserve themselves: Protestant Germany's resistance collapses, and with it a generation's dreams of religious settlement. Pascal, born this year, will eventually argue that both paths — reason and faith — meet in the wager's infinite stakes.
conn.funFact: The Droeshout engraving on the First Folio's title page was made by a twenty-one-year-old who almost certainly never saw Shakespeare alive — he worked from an earlier, now-lost portrait.
